questions.prompt: Silicon is a group IV element. In the silicon crystal (shown in the 2D bond model), how many valence electrons does each atom have, and how many covalent bonds does it form?
options: 4 valence electrons; 4 bonds, one to each nearest neighbour
4 valence electrons; 8 bonds, one per electron it shares or borrows
2 valence electrons (the 3p²); 2 bonds
14 electrons, all of which take part in bonding
questions.explanation:
Silicon's outer shell holds 4 electrons (\(3s^2 3p^2\), which hybridize into 4 \(sp^3\) orbitals in the crystal). Each atom bonds to 4 neighbours in the diamond lattice, and each bond holds 2 electrons: one contributed by each atom (reader Sec. 3.3.2, 3.3.6).
• 8 bonds double-counts: each atom 'sees' 8 electrons around it (4 own + 4 shared), but that is still 4 bonds.
• Only the two 3p electrons bonding would not fill the shell; the hybridized state uses all four.
• The 10 core electrons are tightly bound and never take part in bonding or conduction.

questions.prompt: Pure (undoped) silicon is cooled to \(T = 0\ \mathrm{K}\). How well does it conduct, and why?
options: Very well: each atom has 4 free valence electrons
Moderately: holes conduct even when no bonds are broken
Perfectly: lattice vibrations stop, so there is no scattering
Essentially not at all: every valence electron is locked in a covalent bond, so there are no free carriers
questions.explanation:
At 0 K no bond is broken. The valence band is completely full and the conduction band is empty, so nothing can carry a net current: silicon is an insulator (reader Sec. 3.3.6).
• The 4 valence electrons are the bonding electrons, not free ones (that picture fits a metal's 'electron gas').
• A hole only exists once a bond has been broken.
• Having no scattering doesn't help if there are no carriers to move.

questions.prompt: At room temperature a lattice vibration breaks one Si–Si bond (see figure). What does that create?
options: One free electron only; the lattice stays neutral
Two free electrons, one from each atom of the bond
One free electron and one hole: an electron–hole pair
One hole only; the electron stays bound to its atom
questions.explanation:
The freed electron leaves behind an empty bond site that has net charge \(+q\). A neighbouring bonding electron can hop into it, so the vacancy moves through the crystal like a free positive particle: the hole (Sec. 3.3.7–3.3.8).
Thermal generation always makes carriers in pairs. That is why pure silicon has \(n = p\).

questions.prompt: Silicon's band gap is \(E_g = 1.12\ \mathrm{eV}\). At 300 K the thermal energy is \(kT \approx 26\ \mathrm{meV}\). How many times larger than \(kT\) is the gap? (Give \(E_g/kT\).)
questions.explanation:
\[\frac{E_g}{kT} = \frac{1.12\ \mathrm{eV}}{0.026\ \mathrm{eV}} \approx 43.1\]
An average carrier has far too little energy to cross the gap. Only the rare carriers in the high-energy tail of the thermal distribution make it. That is why silicon has so few free carriers, and why their number depends so strongly (exponentially) on temperature (reader Sec. 3.3.4).

questions.prompt: The reader quotes these conductivities: copper 6.4×10⁷ S/m at 273 K and 4.46×10⁶ S/m at 373 K; germanium 0.5 S/m at 273 K and 833 S/m at 500 K. Which explanation of the opposite temperature trends is right?
options: In both, heating increases scattering, but Ge has more room for its electrons to speed up
In Ge, heating breaks exponentially more bonds, so the carrier count soars; in Cu the carrier count is fixed and more lattice vibration (scattering) lowers the conductivity
Cu loses free electrons as it is heated, while Ge gains mobility
Ge's band gap closes completely above room temperature, turning it into a metal
questions.explanation:
Conductivity is \(\sigma = q(n\mu_n + p\mu_p)\).
• Semiconductor: \(n\) and \(p\) come from thermally broken bonds, \(\propto e^{-E_g/2kT}\). That grows by orders of magnitude, so it swamps the mild drop in mobility.
• Metal: every atom already gives up an electron, so \(n\) is fixed. Heating only adds lattice vibrations (phonons), which shorten the time between collisions and lower \(\mu\).
The gap doesn't close; it shrinks only slightly with temperature.

questions.prompt: Silicon has about \(5\times10^{22}\) atoms per cm³, and at 300 K the free-electron concentration of pure Si is \(n_i = 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\). Each free electron corresponds to one broken bond. What fraction of the atoms have lost an electron (free electrons per atom)? Scientific notation is fine.
questions.explanation:
\[\frac{n_i}{N_{Si}} = \frac{10^{10}}{5\times10^{22}} = 2\times10^{-13}\]
Only about one atom in 5 trillion contributes a free electron at room temperature. Compare a metal, where every atom contributes about one. This is why intrinsic silicon is such a poor conductor.

questions.prompt: A band is completely filled with electrons. The electrons are still moving around inside their bonds. What net current can that band carry when a field is applied?
options: Zero: for a completely filled band, the velocities of all electrons sum to zero
A large current, since it holds the most electrons
A current proportional to the number of electrons, but flowing opposite to the field
Zero at 0 K only; at room temperature its electrons carry current
questions.explanation:
Reader Eq. 3.19: \(\sum_{\text{filled band}} (-q)\,v_i = 0\). In a full band, every state with velocity \(+v\) is paired with a filled state at \(-v\), so the field cannot change the occupation pattern.
Current only appears when the band is partly empty. Writing the partly filled band as 'full band minus missing electrons' gives \(J_{vb} = \sum_{\text{empty}} q\,v_i\) (Eq. 3.21): positive carriers, the holes.
Temperature doesn't change this: a band that stays completely full still gives zero.

questions.prompt: In the bond model, a hole drifts to the RIGHT across the crystal. What are the actual electrons doing, and which way does the conventional current flow?
options: Bonding electrons hop to the RIGHT along with the hole; the current flows to the LEFT
A positive ion core moves to the right; the current flows to the right
Free conduction-band electrons move left; the current flows to the left
Bonding electrons hop one by one to the LEFT into the vacancy; the current flows to the RIGHT
questions.explanation:
Each time a neighbouring valence electron jumps into the empty bond, the vacancy moves one site the opposite way. A hole moving right means a chain of valence electrons, each moving left (reader Fig. 3.11).
Negative charge moving left is the same current as positive charge moving right, so the current points right, along the hole's motion. The ion cores never move, and the hole lives in the valence band, not the conduction band.

questions.prompt: Light can break a Si–Si bond if one photon carries at least the band-gap energy \(E_g = 1.12\ \mathrm{eV}\). Using \(E_{photon} = 1.24/\lambda\) (eV, with \(\lambda\) in µm), what is the LONGEST wavelength that can still create electron–hole pairs in silicon?
questions.explanation:
\[\lambda_{max} = \frac{1.24}{E_g} = \frac{1.24}{1.12} \approx 1.107\ \mu\mathrm{m}\]
Gotcha: a longer wavelength means LESS energy per photon. Photons longer than about 1.1 µm (such as the 1.3 µm and 1.55 µm telecom bands) pass straight through silicon, which is why fibre-optic detectors use other materials. Shorter wavelengths all work; the extra energy above \(E_g\) is lost as heat.

questions.prompt: Preview of intrinsic carrier concentration: a later skill shows that the number of thermally broken bonds scales roughly as \(n_i \propto e^{-E_g/2kT}\). Germanium has \(E_g = 0.66\ \mathrm{eV}\) and silicon \(1.12\ \mathrm{eV}\). Ignoring every other difference between the two, estimate \(n_{i,Ge}/n_{i,Si}\) at 300 K (\(kT = 0.026\ \mathrm{eV}\)).
questions.explanation:
\[\frac{n_{i,Ge}}{n_{i,Si}} = \exp\!\left(\frac{E_{g,Si}-E_{g,Ge}}{2kT}\right) = \exp\!\left(\frac{0.46}{0.052}\right) = e^{8.85} \approx 6948\]
A gap only 0.46 eV smaller gives thousands of times more free carriers. That exponential sensitivity is why the reader's germanium conducts so much better than silicon, and why it is so temperature sensitive. (The measured ratio is about 2×10³ because the prefactors differ; the exponential dominates.)
questions.figure_alt: Plot of the exponential factor e^(−Eg/2kT) versus band gap; germanium at 0.66 eV is far higher than silicon at 1.12 eV.

questions.prompt: Preview of doping: one silicon atom is replaced by phosphorus, a group V element with 5 valence electrons (see figure). In the bond model, what happens?
options: P forms five bonds, so no free carriers appear
P takes an electron from a neighbour, creating a hole
Four of P's electrons form the four bonds; the fifth is barely bound and is easily freed, leaving a fixed positive P⁺ ion
The fifth electron stays bound at room temperature, so nothing changes
questions.explanation:
Only four bonds are available in the diamond lattice. The fifth electron isn't needed for bonding, so at room temperature it is essentially always free. The P atom left behind is a positive ion that cannot move.
This is the idea behind doping: an impurity that donates a free electron without creating a hole (reader Sec. 3.5.1). A group III atom (boron) does the opposite.

questions.prompt: Preview of doping: one silicon atom is replaced by boron, a group III element with only 3 valence electrons. What does the bond model predict?
options: B releases a free electron, leaving a positive ion
B grabs an electron from a neighbouring bond to complete its four bonds, creating a mobile hole and a fixed negative B⁻ ion
B forms only three bonds and the crystal stays neutral with no carriers
B creates an electron–hole pair, like a broken bond
questions.explanation:
With only three electrons, one of B's four bonds is incomplete. An electron from a nearby Si–Si bond fills it. That vacancy moves away as a free hole, and the boron becomes a fixed negative ion (reader Sec. 3.5.3).
Unlike a thermally broken bond, no free electron is created, so the material gains holes only (p-type). Group III dopants are 'acceptors'; group V dopants are 'donors'.
